steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Meta-learning, or learning to learn, means learning the learning algorithm itself, in a similar way to how deep learning replaced handcrafted feature engineering. It is an appealing vision. Meta-learning has found applications in many parts of AI. One notable application is to learn better optimization strategies that optimize better or faster than hand-crafted optimizers. After first succeeding on relatively small scale problems, researchers have recently focused on scaling learned optimizers.

One example is VeLO. It was trained on a huge array of tasks with over 4000 TPU months, and it aims to be a 'foundational' optimizer that can solve any new problem more rapidly than hand-designed optimizers like Adam. VeLO claimed several remarkable abilities, for example being at least 4\times faster than Adam on 50% of tasks in the VeLOdrome suite. If this is true, VeLO would eventually pay for its up-front training cost because it would accelerate learning across the community.

- Evaluating optimizers is hard
  - facets: iteration + time efficiency, quality/generalisation of minima, hyperparameter sensitivity (cite), generalisation of the learned optimiser itself
- This work
  - critically analyse VeLO; doubt on efficacy and on scaling as silver bullet
  - (1) Validation of VeLO: independent evaluation, extended analysis on MLCommons benchmark
  - (2) Claims Reassessment: hyperparameter-free, outperforming baselines on training objectives, speedups
  - (3) Introduction of Explicit Metrics: aligned with optimizer objectives; standardized framework for comparing VeLO to others

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Meta-learning, or learning to learn, means learning the learning algorithm itself, in a similar way to how deep learning replaced handcrafted feature engineering. It is an appealing vision. Meta-learning has found applications in many parts of AI. One notable application is to learn better optimization strategies that optimize better or faster than hand-crafted optimizers. After first succeeding on relatively small scale problems, researchers have recently focused on scaling learned optimizers.

One example is VeLO. It was trained on a huge array of tasks with over 4000 TPU months, and it aims to be a 'foundational' optimizer that can solve any new problem more rapidly than hand-designed optimizers like Adam. VeLO claimed several remarkable abilities, for example being at least 4\times faster than Adam on 50% of tasks in the VeLOdrome suite. If this is true, VeLO would eventually pay for its up-front training cost because it would accelerate learning across the community. However, evaluating optimizers, and learned optimizers especially, is itself a very difficult problem. It has many facets, including iteration and time-efficiency, quality and generalisation of the minima found, hyperparameter sensitivity, and generalisation of the learned optimiser itself.

In this work, we analyse VeLO's performance critically to see if it is as effective as claimed. Our evaluation casts doubt on its claimed efficacy, and on whether scaling up training is the silver bullet for optimizer learning that it has been in other areas of AI. Our contributions are: (1) Validation of VeLO: We do a rigorous, independent evaluation of VeLO's performance with an extended analysis based on the MLCommons benchmark. (2) Claims Reassessment: Our empirical results challenge several key claims of the original VeLO paper, namely that it is hyperparameter-free, that it outperforms baselines in minimizing training objectives, and that it offers optimization speedups. (3) Introduction of Explicit Metrics: We introduce a set of selected metrics that align directly with the fundamental objectives an optimizer should fulfil. These metrics are a standardized framework for comparing VeLO against other optimizers.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Meta-learning, or learning to learn, refers to the appealing vision of learning the learning algorithm itself, similarly to how deep learning replaced handcrafted feature engineering [1]. Meta-learning has found compelling applications in various facets of AI. In particular, one notable application is to learn improved optimization strategies [2] that provide better or faster optimization than hand-crafted optimizers [3]. After initial successes on relatively small scale problems, researchers have recently focused on scaling learned optimizers [4,5].

A noteworthy example is VeLO [5]. Trained on a huge array of tasks with over 4000 TPU months, it aims to be a 'foundational' optimizer capable of solving any new problem more rapidly than hand-designed optimizers such as Adam. VeLO claimed multiple remarkable abilities, such as being at least 4\times faster than Adam on 50% of tasks in the VeLOdrome suite. If true, VeLO would eventually pay for its up-front training cost by accelerating learning across the community. Nevertheless, evaluating optimizers, especially learned optimizers, is itself a very difficult problem with multiple facets, including iteration and time-efficiency, quality and generalisation of the minima discovered, hyperparameter sensitivity [6,3,7], and generalisation of the learned optimiser itself.

In this work, we critically analyse VeLO's performance to understand whether it is as effective as claimed. Our evaluation casts doubt on its claimed efficacy, and on whether scaling up training is the silver bullet for optimizer learning that it has been in other areas of AI. Our contributions are: (1) Validation of VeLO: We conduct a rigorous, independent evaluation of VeLO's performance using an extended analysis based on the MLCommons benchmark. (2) Claims Reassessment: Our empirical results challenge several key claims made in the original VeLO paper, specifically those of being hyperparameter-free, outperforming baselines in minimizing training objectives, and offering optimization speedups. (3) Introduction of Explicit Metrics: We introduce a set of carefully selected metrics that directly align with the fundamental objectives an optimizer should fulfil. These metrics serve as a standardized framework for comparing VeLO against other optimizers.
